newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin gives big boost to Chechnya peace talks.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin gives big boost to Chechnya peace talks.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin, in a surprise change of tactics, ordered on Saturday Russian troops to leave the breakaway region of Chechnya.
Under the order the Interior Ministry's Brigade No 101 and the armed forces' Brigade No 205 were to move out of Chechnya.
Yeltsin's decree, published on the Kremlin press service, did not state any deadline for withdrawal but ordered the government to organise it in a "planned manner".

The document was named "On measures to secure further peaceful settlement in the Chechen Republic". It said it was aimed at "reaching accord in society, furthering a peace settlement and demilitarisation of the Chechen Republic".
Following the August 31 peace deal between Moscow and the rebels, Yeltsin said he was against a hasty troops withdrawal.
Under a series of peace deals earlier this year, most Russian troops have already left Chechnya, scene of 21 months of fierce fighting in which tens of thousands died.
The status of the two brigades remained one of the most controversial outstanding issues between Moscow and the rebels.
Moscow had wanted the two brigades to stay in Chechnya permanently but rebels insisted all Russian troops leave.
Yakov Firsov, a spokesman for Russia's North Caucasus military district, told Reuters the two brigades were the last remaing Russian units in the predominantly Moslem territory.

An Interior Ministry official told Interfax news agency the target for the troops withdrawal was January 27 -- the day of general elections in Chechnya -- but most of the units may leave before the end of the year.
Yeltsin's order was likley to give a boost to talks between Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin and the head of the Chechen rebel government Aslan Maskhadov in Moscow later on Saturday.
A government spokesman said the meeting would be closed to the press and did not give any details.

Russian media reports have said the accord, due to be signed by Chernomyrdin and Maskhadov, mainly covered reconstruction of the region and also included guarantees for tens of thousands of Russians caught up in the fighting that ended with a peace accord signed on August 31.

Despite the progress of their talks, a permanent political settlement remains elusive, with the Chechen side insisting on full independence and Moscow trying to keep the region within the Russian Federation.
